stories.headline: 21 years after 2005 quake, does J&K’s seismic label really matter?
stories.title: 21 years after 2005 quake, does J&K’s seismic label really matter?
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 7: After briefly being placed in a newly created, highest-risk Zone VI seismic zone, Kashmir is back under the older framework. This change did not take place because the earthquake risk decreased, but because the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) withdrew its revised earthquake design code. Twenty-one years after the devastating Kashmir earthquake exposed the vulnerability of buildings across J&K, risks have only accentuated, not mitigated. On March 3, 2026, nearly four months after the BIS had proposed a new Zone VI for much of the Himalayan region, including most of Kashmir, the process was put on hold. This was due to concerns from government agencies and industry stakeholders who worried about the cost and implementation implications of the stricter standards. The new standards meant potentially higher construction costs and constraints on infrastructure and development, especially in vulnerable areas, including Kashmir. This halt restored the earlier seismic classification under which J&K falls in Zones IV and V. The change in classification, however, does not change the geological reality lurking beneath J&K. No comprehensive assessment of Kashmir’s earthquake vulnerability has been carried out. This lacuna and flip-flop of seismic zoning is particularly significant for Kashmir. On October 8, 2005, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake caused extensive destruction across J&K. The official post-earthquake documentation recorded nearly 29,000 houses as fully damaged and more than 83,000 partially damaged. Areas in Uri, Kupwara, Baramulla, Anantnag, Pulwama, and Budgam were worst affected. The same assessment found that poorly built stone and brick structures performed badly under the strong shaking. The absence of earthquake-resistant measures contributed to failures. Two decades later, the question must not be whether J&K is labelled Zone IV, V, or the briefly proposed Zone VI. It must be whether the built environment has become sufficiently resilient to the seismic forces. The government told the J&K Legislative Assembly during its September session that assessment was being carried out by a High-Level Committee for Hazard, Vulnerability and Risk Assessment (HVRA) that was constituted in February 2026. Any plans and policies will follow this assessment, the Government said. A long-term mitigation plan is therefore a far cry in J&K at this point. There is an important distinction between the seismic map and actual vulnerability. A seismic zone describes the hazard framework used for design standards. It does not describe what will happen if an earthquake takes place. The eventual damage also depends on the quality of construction and whether building codes have been adhered to. The local ground conditions and the type of buildings, in addition to the concentration of people in an area as well as the condition and safety standards of critical infrastructure, are equally determinant. A 2026 geotechnical study of Srinagar found that large parts of the city have high to severe susceptibility to earthquake-induced soil liquefaction. This is more of a concern along the Jhelum with loose alluvial deposits and shallow groundwater. The 2025 BIS revision sought to move beyond India's traditional fixed seismic-zone approach. It attempted a more probability-based assessment of ground motion. For J&K, the danger is that the debate becomes reduced to terminology. Zone V versus Zone VI becomes irrelevant when no measures are in place to make J&K more resistant to a seismic disaster.

stories.headline: Assam Government Halts Pay Scale Proposals for Muster Roll Workers Following Supreme Court Ruling
stories.title: Assam Government Halts Pay Scale Proposals for Muster Roll Workers Following Supreme Court Ruling
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

event term: 'supreme court ruling' in title weight 46
article_sentences: Guwahati, Oct 7: The Assam Government has decided not to entertain any new proposals for granting minimum pay scale to muster roll, fixed pay, casual and similarly placed workers, following a Supreme Court's order setting aside a Gauhati High Court judgment that had formed the basis for the benefit.

The Finance Department issued an executive order in this regard on Tuesday, citing the Supreme Court's order dated May 21, 2026, in Civil Appeal No. 4514/2025, Sukhendu Bhattacharjee & Others vs State of Assam & Others, along with seven connected appeals.

In its June 8, 2017 judgment in Writ Appeal No. 45/2014 (State of Assam vs Upen Das & Others), the Gauhati High Court had directed that muster roll, work-charged and similarly placed workers who had completed more than 10 years of service and were not engaged against sanctioned posts should not be terminated until normal retirement, except on disciplinary or criminal grounds.
The court had also directed payment of the minimum applicable pay scale with effect from August 1, 2017.

Following the high court order, the Finance Department had invited proposals from various administrative departments and granted minimum pay scale to eligible workers based on proposals received between May 2019 and September 2026.
However, the Supreme Court, through its May 21, 2026 order, set aside the 2017 Gauhati High Court judgment.
Consequently, the state government has held that claims for minimum pay scale can no longer be sustained on the basis of the apex court judgment.

The Finance Department also stated that adequate opportunities had been provided to departments between October 2017 and September 2025 to submit authenticated lists and checklists of eligible workers.
The decision was approved by the Assam Cabinet on September 24, 2026.

stories.headline: Cabinet expansion within days: CM Omar
stories.title: Cabinet expansion within days: CM Omar
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 7: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Wednesday said the expansion of his council of ministers will take place after he returns from the GST Council meeting in Delhi, following consultations with National Conference President Farooq Abdullah. Responding to a question on the expansion, the chief minister said he had earlier indicated it would happen after the assembly session. "I had said it would happen after the (assembly) session. The session has just concluded. I would have done it during these days, but tomorrow there is a GST Council meeting in Delhi. After completing that and returning, I will consult with Farooq sahab and decide on the next course of action," he said. Speaking to reporters, CM Omar said he was pinning his hopes on the ongoing Supreme Court proceedings to prevent further voter deletions under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), warning of a possibility of "tampering" with elections through the exercise. The SIR is yet to be held in Jammu and Kashmir. "Just as in the rest of the country, this is being done to tamper with elections. It is possible they will attempt to do the same in Jammu and Kashmir. However, we have already been victims of such tampering before. We have not forgotten the delimitation exercise yet. The sole purpose of that delimitation was to help the BJP. The same will likely happen with the SIR," the CM said. He said that the court proceedings, especially those concerning Form 6, would make it "slightly difficult" to remove people from the voter list in J&K. CM Omar also defended the INDIA bloc's escalating agitation against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, questioning the BJP's claim that the allegations against the poll panel are "fabricated". "Where is the fabrication? If it were fabricated, why don't they take action against the newspaper through which all this came to light? I have not seen any defamation suit filed against them anywhere," he said, referring to reports by 'The Indian Express'. The CM argued that the absence of legal action suggested the reports were accurate. On the protests, he said the course of action was decided at a recent INDIA bloc meeting in Delhi. "Kharge sahab announced a month-long calendar before the media, and we are simply taking that forward," CM Omar said. Asked about Prime Minister Narendra Modi completing 25 years in public life, he said he could not review such a long span from where he stood. "He must have done something right for people to have voted for him repeatedly. It is not easy to continuously win elections for 25 years, first at the state level and then at the central level," the CM said, extending congratulations on his own behalf and that of his colleagues. Reacting to the transfers of several bureaucrats by the Lieutenant Governor earlier in the day, he said the postings must have been made thoughtfully. "In our governance setup, what can one say... this is the system. Some changes are made by us, some are made by the LG sahab," CM Omar said, adding that the government would work with the officers in whichever departments they have joined. On the framing of recruitment rules, he said they were "almost ready". The CM said contradictions in the rules drafted and proposed earlier were being resolved. "We didn't want to rush into this only to have counterproductive results. So, even if it takes a couple of days longer, thorough due diligence is being carried out to eliminate any contradictions and legal ambiguities," he said, adding that the rules would be notified "very soon".

stories.headline: J&K GCC Summit 2026: The Arithmetic of a Capability Centre
stories.title: J&K GCC Summit 2026: The Arithmetic of a Capability Centre
stories.summary: Ask the chief financial officer of a Global Capability Centre what it costs to run. The answer begins with people. Salaries, pension, gratuity, power subsidy and social benefits take the largest share of UT's annual budget. That simple fact should shape how Jammu and Kashmir competes for the sector. And that simple fact is what the J&K Government is going to position at the J&K GCC Summit 2026, being organized by the Government of J&K and IIM Jammu. If a capability centre is a ten-year commitment to recurring cost, the location decision turns on what the centre will cost to run in its fifth and eighth years, discounted to today. The one-time cost of setting up is a minor line in that calculation. We have 55 investors from the world's leading Fortune 500 GCC and GCC- enabling companies and India's leading multinationals descending at IIM Jammu on 9-10 October for the Summit. And each one of them perhaps already knows that a capital subsidy, however generous, only addresses the smallest part of the problem. A subsidy is easy to announce, and it makes good PR. But what moves a location decision is sustained relief on recurring cost. That means employment- linked support for each professional hired and retained, a defined share of payroll cost reimbursed for a limited period, lease rental assistance, electricity tariff subsidy, stamp duty relief on leases and a grant for each candidate trained and placed. Outcome-linked support also has a fiscal property that capital subsidies lack. Its cost rises only when jobs rise. The exposure of the exchequer is therefore bounded by success and can be budgeted year by year against verified employment. A capital subsidy is paid at the start, whatever happens afterwards. Recovering it from a nucleus that underperforms is slow and uncertain. Retention is the second variable. Here Jammu and Kashmir holds a structural advantage. Consider an illustrative centre of 500 professionals. At an annual attrition rate of 20 per cent it must replace 100 people every year. At 10 per cent it replaces 50. Over a decade, the difference is 500 replacements, equivalent to rebuilding the entire centre once over. Each replacement carries the cost of recruitment, training and months of reduced productivity. Professionals who work in Jammu and Kashmir are, for the most part, working where their families live. The pull of a marginally better offer across town, which drives much of the churn in metropolitan clusters, operates with far less force here. Add office, talent and utility costs well below metropolitan levels, and the Union Territory has a cost position that rests on its own fundamentals. The competition is real. At least eight States have notified dedicated GCC policies, from Karnataka, which moved first, to Haryana in May 2026. Tamil Nadu addresses the sector through a dedicated framework and Andhra Pradesh through its IT policy. Their incentive menus vary widely. So do the thresholds at which benefits begin. A Union Territory without an existing GCC base cannot borrow a threshold designed for a mature cluster. It must set thresholds that a first entrant can realistically meet. J&K's GCC Policy has been drafted and will be showcased to the prospective GCC multinationals that are attending the J&K GCC Summit. These multinationals will benchmark J&K against the above expected benefits. Be that as it may, we should assess support for the sector in J&K against five rules. First, pay for outcomes. Support from the J&k Government should be attached to jobs created and sustained, payroll actually paid and candidates actually placed, each verified against EPFO and ESIC records, the exchequer may pay for delivery and only after it. Second, setting a horizon. Every incentive should reduce over time and end on a known date, so that a centre's economics is tested on its own profitability rather than continuing purely because of support. Third, avoid paying twice. A Union Territory instrument should fill the gaps left by Central and Union Territory schemes already in force for industry and skilling, chiefly on operating and lease cost and not vice versa. Fourth, weigh the return. At an illustrative average salary of R10 lakh a year, a centre of 500 professionals pays R50 crore in salaries every year, much of it spent locally. It pays stamp duty on its leases. Its local spending and the consumption of its employees generate GST. It supports a comparable number of indirect jobs in facilities, transport and hospitality. For a Union Territory working to strengthen its own revenue base, a sector whose spending stays local is fiscally attractive. Fifth, publish the ledger. The incentives paid, and the jobs verified against them should be disclosed every year. Transparency is the cheapest way to sustain public confidence in industrial incentives. But then, the caveat is that no incentive can compensate for an unclear approval timeline, a building that is yet to be built or a talent pipeline that falls short of an employer's requirement. And that is where the J&K Government is ensuring that investors, and not just from the GCC ecosystem, are provided clear approval timelines, assessed and industry-ready talent pool and infrastructure that is plug- and-play ready than bare land. As I mentioned earlier, the J&K GCC Summit 2026 at IIM Jammu on 9 and 10 October gives the Union Territory a rare opportunity to hear from operators what actually can work for us to be considered as the emerging destination for GCCs. Join the conversation and give us your inputs on what may work. Well, this is a first step, and we hope one that goes a million miles. (The writer is Additional Chief Secretary, Finance Department, Government of Jammu and Kashmir)

stories.headline: The Gateway Paradox
stories.title: The Gateway Paradox
stories.summary: TECHNOLOGY & NATIONAL SECURITY Kashmir knows what it is to lose a connection by order. India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, according to Access Now, and in Jammu and Kashmir the authorities went after VPN users under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, penalising roughly 800 people. Satellite broadband looks like the answer. A dish on a rooftop in a high-altitude village needs no local tower and no fibre run. In early September, the Digital Communications Commission approved a spectrum framework that moves Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio’s satellite venture closer to commercial launch. But a network with no towers still has a throat. Every one of these services must land its traffic at a gateway on Indian soil, and whoever controls the gateway controls the switch. What the framework approves, and what it does not According to MediaNama, the commission cleared TRAI’s recommendations on 3 September. Spectrum would be assigned for five years, with a possible two-year extension, at 5 per cent of adjusted gross revenue. Operators serving rural and remote areas may get a 4 per cent rate. The Department of Telecommunications rejected a proposed Rs 500 annual levy on urban subscribers. Three steps remain: Union Cabinet approval, formal spectrum assignment, and security clearance from the Ministry of Home Affairs. The draft spectrum rules reported in June go further. They require government approval before consumer services launch, and they require authorisation to connect a satellite network to public telecom infrastructure. Starlink’s own plans show where the weight sits. MediaNama reports about 20 earth stations across Noida, Chennai and Navi Mumbai, a capacity of up to 2 million users, and a terminal costing around Rs 33,000. Two million connections would run through a few facilities in three cities. A shutdown that moves from the tower to the gateway Today, a suspension order in Kashmir lands on telecom operators and their local infrastructure, district by district. It is blunt, and it is visible. Satellite links change the mechanics. If traffic for a whole footprint passes through a handful of gateways, one lawful order to one facility could darken a large area at once. “The dish on the roof is hard to cut. The gateway in Noida is easy to switch off.” That is my inference, and it has limits. The licence conditions that would govern gateway shutdowns are not public, and I could not verify whether they allow targeted, area-by-area suspension. What is public is the direction. MediaNama reported in June that security agencies under the Home Ministry had frozen Starlink’s final clearances and wanted monitoring systems inside India and regular reporting to law enforcement. Starlink disputed the freeze and called its talks with the government “active and productive”. The design has a security logic. A gateway on Indian soil is the only place where Delhi can enforce anything against a foreign operator. It is also the place where a promise of shutdown-proof connectivity gets tested. The beam does not read maps MediaNama also reports that agencies are examining signal spillover near the borders. A satellite footprint over the Valley does not stop at the Line of Control. The same constellation that serves Gurez serves territory on the other side. Terminals add a second worry. The Indian Army recovered what it described as a Starlink device with weapons in Manipur in December 2024, per MediaNama, and terminals worked in Iran during that country’s conflict without proper licensing. A Rs 33,000 terminal fits in a rucksack. The state’s likely response is tighter control at the two points it can reach: the gateway and the terminal registry. Both are felt first by the legitimate user in a remote district. The smuggler who skips the registry still depends on a gateway that will carry the traffic, which is why the location of that gateway matters so much to security agencies. The steelman Keeping gateways in India is better than the alternative. A foreign operator running a network over Indian territory with no domestic control point would be a sovereignty problem of a different kind, and the Iran episode shows why agencies worry. Satellite links also survive physical damage that would take a tower or a cable offline, and that has real value in a region of floods and snowfall. So the argument is narrower. Resilience and control are being sold as one product, and they are two. The first protects users from accidents. The second protects the state from users, and the licence conditions will decide which one dominates. Bottom Line Satellite broadband will make India’s border regions harder to cut off by accident. It will also make them easier to switch off on purpose, from a few buildings in Noida, Chennai and Navi Mumbai. Before the Cabinet signs off, Delhi should publish the conditions under which a gateway can be ordered dark, and say who reviews that order. Kashmir has lived with the unpublished version for long enough. (The Author studies Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence at Rutgers University, New Jersey, USA. He is interested in emerging technologies and innovation, and can be reached on LinkedIn at @arssh-kumar14)

stories.headline: 20 years on, J&K's small hydro potential largely untapped
stories.title: 20 years on, J&K's small hydro potential largely untapped
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 7: Twenty years after Jammu and Kashmir first invited private companies to build small hydropower plants, most of the region's potential still flows downstream unused. The Comptroller and Auditor General has identified 374 sites in J&K suitable for small hydro projects, together worth about 1725 megawatts. Only 12 privately built projects, with a combined capacity of roughly 93.75 MW, are running today. Small hydro plants generate up to 25 MW. They need no big dam. A portion of a stream is diverted through a pipe and a turbine, then returned to the channel. 1 policy that worked, 3 that didn't The government has tried four times to draw in private investment. Only the first attempt delivered plants at any scale. The 2003 Small Hydro Policy offered projects of up to 25 MW on a 40-year term, a modest upfront fee and no free power to the state for the first 15 years. Twelve projects were allotted and five were built, producing 57.5 MW. That is more than was originally advertised, as some developers found more water at their sites than expected. The 2011 Hydro Policy, run by the J&K State Power Development Corporation, took a harder line. It raised fees, demanded a larger share of free power from day one and shortened the lease period. Developers say the terms made projects difficult to finance. No new private project has come up under it in fifteen years. A separate 2011 policy for mini and micro projects of up to 2 MW, run by the J&K Energy Development Agency, fared little better. More than 100 projects were tendered, but only seven are operating. The latest draft Hydro Policy was announced in March 2025 and is still awaiting approval. Developers say the draft meets many of their long-standing demands. They fear, however, that the final changes are being made without proper consultation, the same mistake they say was made in 2011. Chief Minister Omar Abdullah recently called for a focused policy framework for the sector, but investors say fresh money is unlikely until a policy is notified and seen to be stable. The water charge The biggest sticking point is the water usage charge. J&K began levying 25 paise per cubic metre on water passing through power plants in 2010. No other state was doing so at the time. The charge was aimed mainly at large central projects, but it also reached small private plants, including some that had been promised exemptions. Because it is billed on the volume of water and not on the electricity sold, the levy can eat up a large part of a small plant's income. Since 2023 the Union Ministry of Power has advised states to withdraw such charges on power generation. The High Courts of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand have struck down similar levies in their states. In J&K the matter is before the courts, and until it is settled banks regard small hydro as a risky bet. The money trail is also awkward for the state. NHPC, the central generator, went to the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission in 2011 seeking to recover the J&K water charges and licence fee through its tariff, naming northern utilities such as Punjab and Haryana as respondents. Having won the relief, it passed the cost on to its buyers. By one count, NHPC has paid J&K Rs 2,062.51 crore in water charges, including Rs 701.53 crore in 2011-12 alone. J&K is itself a large buyer of NHPC power, so part of that money came back through higher power purchase bills. The state later amended its law so the water charge fund could be used to meet the higher cost of power bought from suppliers who had revised their tariffs. In effect, a levy that was meant to build new hydro capacity ended up paying for power bills, while small developers were left with a charge they had no way of recovering. Solar, shrinking rivers, neighbours ahead Small hydro is also competing with solar for investors' money. India added about 44.6 GW of solar capacity in 2025-26 alone. A solar park can be built in about two years with fewer approvals and no river studies. A small hydro project in J&K has to offer clearer and steadier terms to compete for the same capital. Time is not on its side either. Glaciers in the Upper Jhelum basin have shrunk by about a fifth, and University of Kashmir studies have recorded falling stream flows since the mid-1990s. Early last year the Jhelum touched one of its lowest levels on record. Unlike coal or oil, river water cannot be stored for later use, and what is not used simply flows away. Neighbouring hill states have meanwhile moved ahead. Himachal Pradesh has more than ten times the capacity that J&K's privately built small hydro plants have. Observers put the gap down largely to clear rules, steady terms and a simple path from allotment to generation. Consumers carry cost For households, the stalled sector shows up in the monthly bill. J&K spent about Rs 55,254 crore on power purchases over a decade. About 44 percent of the electricity in the region is lost in the network or never paid for, against a national average of around 16 percent. Tariffs went up by an average of 6.83 per cent from September 1. Local plants built at the far ends of the grid would offer jobs in remote villages, free power for the government and lower transmission losses, since electricity generated close to where it is used travels less. None is being added at any meaningful pace. There is some help on the way from the Centre. A new scheme has set aside Rs 2,584.60 crore for small hydro across the country from 2026 to 2031, with extra support for hill and border areas. J&K can benefit, but only once its own policy is in place. What industry wants Developers and industry representatives point to four steps. They want the new policy finalised after consultation with developers and banks, and the water charge question settled in line with the Union's advice and court rulings elsewhere, with earlier exemptions honoured. They also want projects sized according to what each stream can carry, instead of by fixed limits, and the central scheme used to fund project reports and support projects in remote and border districts. "We have already lost 20 years," is how many in the sector put it. With the rivers carrying less water each year, they say, there is little room for another lost decade.

stories.headline: September rains falter across J&K, Ladakh; Kashmir 33%, Jammu 21% below normal
stories.title: September rains falter across J&K, Ladakh; Kashmir 33%, Jammu 21% below normal
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 7: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh recorded a significant rainfall deficit in September, with 20 districts receiving 1337.6 mm against a combined normal of 1768.7 mm, a shortfall of 431.1 mm, or 24.4 percent. According to India Meteorological Department (IMD) data, Kashmir recorded a 33.4 percent deficit, Jammu 21.4 percent, and Ladakh 97.8 percent. The combined 20-district shortfall of 24.4 percent falls in the IMD’s deficit category. Under IMD classification, rainfall departures of minus 19 percent to 19 percent are normal, minus 20 percent to minus 59 percent are deficit and below minus 60 percent are large deficit. Departures of 20 percent to 59 percent are excess and 60 percent or more are large excess. Kashmir’s eight districts received 252.8 mm against 379.6 mm normal, a 33.4 percent deficit. Badgam recorded the Valley’s steepest shortfall at 65 percent, a large deficit, with 16.3 mm against 46.0 mm normal. Kupwara recorded a 54 percent deficit (16.8/36.3 mm), Kulgam 51 percent (34.8/71.3 mm), Bandipora 41 percent (17.0/28.7 mm), and Ganderbal 35 percent (42.4/65.2 mm). Anantnag was 24 percent below normal (45.7/60.4 mm), while Pulwama was 4 percent below normal (31.9/33.2 mm). Baramulla was the only Kashmir district with excess rainfall, recording 25 percent above normal (47.9/38.5 mm). Jammu’s 10 districts received 1084.6 mm against 1380.0 mm normal, a 21.4 percent deficit. Samba recorded the steepest shortfall in the region at 92 percent, with just 11.5 mm against 147.6 mm normal. Doda recorded a 69 percent deficit (27.0/88.3 mm), Ramban 65 percent (31.1/89.0 mm) and Kishtwar 60 percent (35.0/88.3 mm). Rajouri was 25 percent below normal (108.3/145.0 mm), while Poonch was 9 percent below (116.0/128.0 mm), Reasi 4 percent below (198.1/205.9 mm), and Jammu 3 percent below (110.3/114.0 mm). Kathua received 15 percent more than normal rainfall (228.3/198.2 mm), remaining within the IMD’s normal category, while Udhampur recorded a 25 percent surplus (219.0/175.7 mm), classified as excess. In Ladakh, Leh and Kargil received just 0.2 mm against a combined normal of 9.1 mm, a 97.8 percent large deficit. Kargil recorded no rainfall against its 2.5-mm normal, while Leh received 0.2 mm against 6.6 mm normal, a 97 percent deficit. The rainfall pattern varied sharply with elevation. Higher reaches witnessed intense showers and occasional cloudbursts, while lower areas generally received light to moderate rain. Some intense spells triggered flash floods, landslides, mudslides, shooting stones and rockfalls. September followed a mixed summer rainfall pattern. J&K recorded a 24 percent deficit in June, followed by 35 percent excess rainfall in July, bringing cumulative June-August precipitation into the normal category despite another shortfall in August. In August, Kashmir recorded a 25 percent deficit and Jammu 16 percent below normal, while Ladakh recorded a 2 percent surplus. All three remained within the IMD’s normal category. Director Meteorological Centre J&K Mukhtar Ahmad said El Niño had started affecting J&K in August and may have contributed to the August and September deficits. He attributed the shortfall largely to reduced Western Disturbance activity. “One or two active spells of Western Disturbances might reverse everything as far as precipitation is concerned,” Ahmad said. For October, Ahmad said the forecast suggests normal precipitation overall, with two to three Western Disturbances expected to bring light to moderate rain to the Kashmir plains and light snowfall over higher reaches. The March-May period had also remained deficient, with J&K recording 28 percent below-normal rainfall. Kashmir recorded a 36 percent deficit, Jammu 20 percent, and Ladakh 26 percent excess.

opening: Srinagar, Oct 7: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh recorded a significant rainfall deficit in September, with 20 districts receiving 1337.6 mm against a combined normal of 1768.7 mm, a shortfall of 431.1 mm, or 24.4 percent.
The combined 20-district shortfall of 24.4 percent falls in the IMD’s deficit category.
body: Departures of 20 percent to 59 percent are excess and 60 percent or more are large excess.
The rainfall pattern varied sharply with elevation.
Higher reaches witnessed intense showers and occasional cloudbursts, while lower areas generally received light to moderate rain.
Some intense spells triggered flash floods, landslides, mudslides, shooting stones and rockfalls.
September followed a mixed summer rainfall pattern.
All three remained within the IMD’s normal category.
Director Meteorological Centre J&K Mukhtar Ahmad said El Niño had started affecting J&K in August and may have contributed to the August and September deficits.
He attributed the shortfall largely to reduced Western Disturbance activity.
“One or two active spells of Western Disturbances might reverse everything as far as precipitation is concerned,” Ahmad said.

bullets.text: For October, Ahmad said the forecast suggests normal precipitation overall, with two to three Western Disturbances expected to bring light to moderate rain to the Kashmir plains and light snowfall over higher reaches.
